headline: S. 311 would have set care and reporting rules for infants born alive after an abortion or attempted abortion, with criminal penalties and a civil damages right for women who had an abortion.
what_it_does: The bill would require a health care practitioner present at such a birth to give the child the same degree of care given to any other child born alive at the same gestational age, and to immediately admit the child to a hospital. Practitioners or other employees would have to report any failure to follow these rules to law enforcement. Violators would face a fine, up to five years in prison, or both, and anyone who intentionally killed or attempted to kill a born-alive child could be prosecuted for murder. The bill would also bar prosecuting a mother of such a child for conspiracy, being an accessory after the fact, or concealment of a felony tied to these provisions, and would let a woman who had an abortion or attempted abortion sue violators for damages.

who_it_affects.group: Health care practitioners, such as doctors and nurses, who attend births after an abortion or attempted abortion
who_it_affects.how: They would have to provide the same level of care as for other born-alive children of the same gestational age, admit the child to a hospital immediately, and report any noncompliance to law enforcement.
They would have to immediately report any failure to comply with the care requirements to law enforcement.

who_it_affects.group: Infants born alive after an abortion or attempted abortion
who_it_affects.how: They would be entitled to the same degree of care as other born-alive children of the same gestational age and to immediate hospital admission.

who_it_affects.group: Women who have had an abortion or attempted abortion
who_it_affects.how: They could file a civil lawsuit for damages against individuals who violated the bill.

who_it_affects.group: Mothers of children born alive after an abortion or attempted abortion
who_it_affects.how: They would be shielded from criminal prosecution for conspiracy, being an accessory after the fact, or concealment of felony connected to these provisions.
